Call script (6–8 Qs — core answer; if‑pressed): 1) Backups/DR in C? — Yes: primary production and backups are hosted in C (provider‑confirmed); if pressed: some DR/replication and legacy failover paths are still being validated and we will provide specifics in the executive packet. 2) Subprocessors in C? — Known analytics/support subprocessors operate from C and are listed in the updated map; if pressed: a small number of legacy/third‑party entries remain pending vendor confirmation. 3) Incomplete legacy flows? — Several legacy integration flows remain under review and could affect scope; if pressed: we will flag any that prove material in the DPIA. 4) Any processing outside what 2022 described? — No evidence of systemic out‑of‑scope processing today, caveated by incomplete map entries; if pressed: we will notify promptly if the DPIA reveals material variance. 5) Register/DPIA status and timing? — Executive transfer register and DPIA summary in 10 business days; full DPIA/register targeted in ~4–6 weeks subject to third‑party confirmations. 6) Pause onboarding? — Not broadly; we will apply targeted holds only if DPIA identifies specific material risks. 7) Mitigations now? — SCCs/contractual clauses, encryption, RBAC, logging and minimization are in place; if pressed: offer a focused technical briefing.  
Variation answer options (three defensible scripts): (A) Cautious — “We are still assessing whether a variation is required and will advise once the DPIA/register are finalised.” (B) Middle (recommended for most use) — “At present we do not consider a formal variation necessary while we validate documentation, but we will promptly engage if the DPIA indicates otherwise.” (C) Business‑forward — “On the current evidence we do not presently expect a variation will be needed; this remains subject to the final DPIA/register.”  
Internal briefing note (short): Firm “no variation” — pros: protects launch timing, reduces immediate regulatory friction; cons: if DPIA later shows material out‑of‑scope transfers this could create credibility/exposure and trigger enforcement or a forced variation. Softer “still assessing” — pros: preserves candour, reduces risk of inconsistency with future findings and aligns with Jurisdiction A’s FAQ; cons: may invite deeper scrutiny and requests that could slow renewal. Recommendation: use the softer formulation on the call (we are still assessing), immediately commit to the 10‑business‑day executive packet and the 4–6‑week DPIA target, accelerate vendor confirmations, and only state “no variation necessary” in writing if the final DPIA/register support that conclusion.  
Caveats/flags: explicitly caveat any claim that the 2022 authorisation “covers” all transfers until legacy integration entries and outstanding subprocessor confirmations are closed; avoid promising tighter timelines than vendor‑dependent targets; clear External Counsel review is required before any written “no variation” assertion.  
Two short BU lines for the opening (non‑technical): “Our production and backups are hosted in Jurisdiction C and we’re committed to delivering an executive transfer register and DPIA summary in 10 business days; we are not pausing launch overall but will pause specific onboarding streams only if the DPIA identifies material issues.”
